note: This is Poll's own published account of the Croatia v Australia error, repeated in his autobiography, so the explanation is his rather than a legend about him.

q: A Liverpool engineer patented the goal net in 1889 after watching a disallowed goal at Everton. What else did he later help build?
a: The Mersey road tunnel, he was John Alexander Brodie
note: Patent November 1889 and the Queensway Mersey Tunnel both confirmed on the Wikipedia article. The disallowed goal (Everton v Accrington, 26 October 1889) is the traditional account and is well sourced, though one history notes he was already working on the idea, which does not affect the answer.

q: The Euro 1968 semi-final between Italy and the Soviet Union finished goalless after 120 minutes. How was it decided?
a: A coin toss, which Italy's Giacinto Facchetti won by calling tails
note: The UEFA page blocks fetching, but its content is quoted elsewhere including Facchetti's own words: he went to the dressing room with the Soviet captain and called tails.

q: Juventus played in pink until 1903, when an English player in the side wrote home for new shirts. Which club's colours turned up?
a: Notts County's black and white stripes
note: Juventus and Notts County both tell this version officially, and the two clubs marked its centenary together, so it is club-confirmed rather than blog folklore. Retiered ball to extreme, the Notts County link is widely known and the question already narrows it to England.

q: With the ball at his feet in the box and the Everton keeper down injured in 2000, what did Paolo Di Canio do?
a: Caught the ball so the keeper could be treated, and won the FIFA Fair Play award for it
note: West Ham at Everton, December 2000, keeper Paul Gerrard injured; the FIFA Fair Play award followed in 2001. Retiered ball to extreme, the catch is one of the best known fair play moments in the English game.

q: In 2002 Norwegian club Flekkerøy signed striker Kenneth Kristensen for one kilo of seafood per kilo of player. What was the final fee?
a: 75 kilos of shrimp, weighed out at a boxing-style weigh-in
note: Checked including the weigh-in detail: Kristensen moved from Vindbjart to Floey, weighed about 75kg, and the shrimp were measured against him at a boxing-style weigh-in before a game.

q: The joint manager who took Iceland to Euro 2016 and beat England had another job. What was it?
a: Dentist, Heimir Hallgrímsson still ran a practice
note: Hallgrimsson was co-manager with Lars Lagerback at Euro 2016 and kept his dental practice in Vestmannaeyjar; widely reported at the time. Retiered ball to extreme, the dentist line was everywhere during that tournament.

q: The Faroe Islands beat Austria 1-0 in their first ever competitive match in 1990. What was their goalkeeper Jens Martin Knudsen wearing?
a: A white bobble hat, worn ever since a head injury as a boy
note: Sources split on whether the concussion was at 13 or 14, so I cut the age rather than bet the answer on it. The hat, the reason and the 1-0 in Landskrona on 12 September 1990 all check out.

q: Heerenveen trailed Ajax 5-1 with half an hour left on 7 May 1950 and won 6-5. Which Frisian folk hero dragged them back?
note: Cut who scored three. Dutch accounts of the goal sequence credit Lenstra with one goal plus the won penalty, with Brandsma scoring twice and Hofma once, even where the same piece says three in prose. The comeback from 5-1 after an hour is right.

q: Ajax were thrown out of Europe for a year in 1989 after a UEFA Cup tie against Austria Wien was abandoned. What had been thrown at the Austrian keeper?
a: An iron rod, from the F-side
note: Has its own Wikipedia article: the rod thrown at Franz Wohlfahrt in December 1989 and the resulting European ban.

q: Go Ahead Eagles were founded in 1902 under a different English name. What was it before the Dutch FA made them change?
note: True (Be Quick until the KNVB made them change in 1905) but it duplicates the hardcore ball question with the same answer. One of the two has to go and the hardcore version is the cleaner ask.

q: Go Ahead Eagles won the KNVB Cup in 2025, their first major trophy since 1933. Who did they beat, and how?
a: AZ, on penalties after a 1-1 draw
note: First major trophy ever was flat wrong: Go Ahead were Dutch champions four times, last in 1933, which another question in this same pack asks about. The 2025 final itself checks out, 21 April at De Kuip, 1-1 with a Deijl penalty deep in stoppage time, 4-2 on penalties.

q: Uruguayan striker Sebastián Abreu holds a Guinness record no manager wants on a CV. What for?
a: Most clubs played for, more than 30
note: Guinness-certified at 31 clubs on retirement in 2021, so more than 30 is safe and the record is closed by his retirement.

q: A three-match World Cup qualifier in 1969 helped tip two countries into a four day shooting war. Which two?
note: Britannica's own entry, and the 100-hour duration matches the four days in the question. Retiered ball to extreme, the Football War is standard reading for anyone with an interest in the game's history.

q: Thomas Helmer's shot in 1994 went wide but was given as a goal, and Bayern beat Nürnberg. What did the German FA do about it?
a: Ordered the match replayed, and Bayern won that 5-0 as well
note: Bayern's own retrospective on the Phantomtor: 2-1 annulled, replay ordered, Bayern won the replay 5-0.

q: Manchester United came out for the second half at Southampton in 1996 in a different kit. What was Alex Ferguson's reason?
a: His players could not pick each other out in the grey shirts
note: April 1996, 3-0 down at half time, changed into blue and white; Ferguson's visibility explanation is on the record. Retiered ball to extreme, the grey kit excuse is part of standard Premier League folklore.

q: Kanu did not realise the ball had been kicked out for an injury and set up Arsenal's winner against Sheffield United in the 1999 FA Cup. What did Arsène Wenger do?
a: Offered to replay the whole tie, and Arsenal won that 2-1 as well
note: Fifth round, February 1999, 2-1 both times; the offer and the FA accepting it are on Arsenal's own site.

q: Robbie Fowler won a UEFA Fair Play award in 1997 for telling the referee that David Seaman had not fouled him. How did it end?
a: The penalty stood, Seaman saved it, and Jason McAteer scored the rebound
note: March 1997 at Highbury; referee Gerald Ashby kept the penalty, Seaman saved, McAteer followed up. Well documented on video.

q: England captain Bobby Moore was arrested in Bogotá in 1970 for stealing a bracelet. What killed the case against him?
a: The blazer she said he had slipped it into had no pocket on that side
note: The tracksuit with no pockets is embroidery. The cited article is specific: in the re-enactment the shop assistant said Moore put the bracelet in his blazer's left-hand pocket, and the blazer had no pocket on that side, at which point her story fell apart.

q: Garrincha won two World Cups with a body that should have stopped him. What was wrong with his legs?
a: They were bent, both knees turned the same way, and one leg was several centimetres shorter than the other
note: Retiered ball to extreme, the bent legs are part of the standard Garrincha story. Cut the polio causation. Britannica says childhood polio, but the orthopaedic literature on his case says he was born with the deformities and polio only worsened them, and sources also disagree on which leg was shorter. The shape of the legs is not disputed, so the answer now sticks to that.

q: Before Argentina played Italy in Naples at the 1990 World Cup, what did Maradona ask the Neapolitans to remember?
a: That the rest of Italy did not treat them as Italians, so they should back Argentina
note: His pre-match remarks are quoted consistently across contemporary and later coverage. Retiered ball to extreme, anyone who knows the Maradona and Naples story can reason their way to it.

q: Barcelona were beaten 11-1 by Real Madrid in a 1943 cup semi-final after leading the tie 3-0. What had happened in their dressing room beforehand?
a: Franco's director of state security had come in to remind them they played only by the regime's generosity
note: The 3-0 first leg and 11-1 second are certain. The dressing room visit is contested history rather than proven fact, but the question asks what happened by the accepted account, and the cited article carries it with sourcing.

q: Jan Jongbloed kept goal for the Netherlands in the 1974 and 1978 World Cup finals. Which shirt number did he wear?
note: He wore 8 in both tournaments under the Dutch alphabetical-ish squad numbering; consistent across squad lists for 1974 and 1978.

q: At the 1978 World Cup a Dutch defender became the first man to score at both ends in the same World Cup match. Who?
note: FIFA's own archive piece, written when Mandzukic became the second to do it, names Brandts and the 1978 Italy game.

q: Brian Clough turned up late to unveil Britain's first million pound player in 1979 carrying what?
a: A squash racket, and wearing a tracksuit, to play the whole thing down
note: The Trevor Francis unveiling is documented in photographs, which settles the racket and the tracksuit.

q: Cameroon were fined and docked six qualifying points in 2004 over their kit. What was wrong with it?
a: It was a one piece bodysuit, and FIFA required shirt and shorts to be separate items
note: Six points and a 154,000 dollar fine confirmed in contemporary reporting. Worth knowing at the table that both punishments were later withdrawn after Puma challenged them, but the question only asks what was wrong with the kit.

q: Mexico goalkeeper Jorge Campos wore neon kits he had designed himself. What else did he do that keepers do not?
a: Played as a forward, scoring 14 league goals in a season for Pumas
note: Checked the 14: blocked behind Adolfo Rios, he asked to play up front and scored 14 in his first season at Pumas.

q: German goalkeeper Lutz Pfannenstiel spent 101 days in a Singapore prison and stopped breathing three times on a pitch in Bradford. What is he officially the only footballer to have done?
a: Played professionally in all six FIFA confederations, the first man to do it
note: Only is stronger than the record actually says. Wikipedia calls him the first footballer to play in all six confederations, so I matched that wording. The 101 days and the Bradford collision both check out.

q: Who holds the record for the fastest booking in English football, carded three seconds into a game against Sheffield United in 1992?
note: Retiered ball to extreme, the three second booking is a well known record and the answer is a household name. Removed FA Cup tie. The sources genuinely conflict: Chelsea's own site says an FA Cup fifth round tie in February 1992, other records put it in a league game on 21 March 1992, and Wikipedia even says five seconds rather than three. Opponent, year and player are agreed, so the question now rests only on those.

q: Referee Damián Rubino set a Guinness record in an Argentine fourth division match in 2011. What for?
a: Sending off 36 players, every player and substitute from both sides
note: Claypole v Victoriano Arenas, February 2011, Guinness-certified at 36.

q: The 1923 FA Cup final, the first at Wembley, started 45 minutes late. Who is credited with clearing the pitch?
a: A police horse called Billie, and PC George Scorey
note: The White Horse Final; both the horse's name and Scorey are on the Wikipedia article, as is the 45 minute delay.

q: Japan's King Kazu, Kazuyoshi Miura, has played professional football in five different decades. Which Brazilian club did he start at in 1986?
note: Still a registered professional at 58 has already gone stale: he turned 59 in February 2026, is on loan at Fukushima United until June 2027 and scored for them in July 2026. Swapped in the five decades framing, which is true and cannot expire. Santos in 1986 confirmed.

q: Referee Clive Thomas never worked another World Cup after Brazil against Sweden in 1978. What did he do?
a: Blew for full time while a corner was in the air, disallowing Zico's header
note: 1-1, Thomas ended the game as Nelinho's corner came in and Zico headed it home; he refereed at 1974 and 1978 and was never selected again.

q: The 2004 Manchester United win that ended Arsenal's 49 match unbeaten run has a nickname. What flew at Alex Ferguson in the tunnel?
a: A slice of pizza, hence the Battle of the Buffet
note: Has its own Wikipedia article, and Cesc Fabregas has since admitted throwing it. Retiered ball to extreme, the pizza is common knowledge and the nickname gives it away.

q: A women's club match at Goodison Park in 1920 drew 53,000, with thousands locked out. What did the FA do a year later?
a: Banned women from playing on the grounds of its member clubs, a ban that lasted until 1971
note: Boxing Day 1920, 53,000 in and around 10,000 locked out, FA ban December 1921 and lifted in 1971; all on the match's own article.

q: Celtic won the European Cup in 1967 with a squad that shared one unusual thing. What?
a: Every player was born within 30 miles of Celtic Park
note: Checked the wording risk. The 30 mile claim holds for the whole 15-man squad, not just the eleven, with Bobby Lennox from Saltcoats the furthest out at about 30 miles.

q: Before settling on football, Lev Yashin was good enough at another sport to win a national cup in 1953. Which?
a: Ice hockey, as a goalkeeper for Dynamo Moscow
note: Fetched the Yashin article: Soviet Cup in 1953 in goal for Dynamo's ice hockey side, and he gave the sport up in 1954.

q: One man has played in two World Cup finals for two different countries. Who?
a: Luis Monti, for Argentina in 1930 and Italy in 1934
note: FIFA's own article; still unique, and the oriundi route that made it possible no longer exists in the same form.

q: At Corinthians in the early 1980s, Sócrates and his teammates ran the club by vote. What were they voting on?
a: Everything, from the team selection to wages and travel, one man one vote including the kit man
note: Corinthians Democracy is documented in detail, including the one man one vote principle extending to non-playing staff.

q: The 1980 Copa del Rey final was a Madrid derby of an odd kind. Who did Real Madrid beat 6-1?
a: Real Madrid Castilla, their own reserve team
note: True, but the hardcore file already asks the year and the score of this same final, so this is a third bite at one match. Dropped as the duplicate.

q: Ruud Gullit won the Ballon d'Or in 1987 and dedicated it to a man in prison. Who?
note: Gullit's own account on the Laureus site, and it matches the contemporary record including the Mandela dedication of his 1988 hit South Africa.

q: The 2001 UEFA Cup final between Liverpool and Alavés finished 5-4 on a golden goal. Who scored it?
a: Delfí Geli of Alavés, into his own net
note: Straight duplicate of the hardcore ball question on the same own goal. Kept the hardcore one.

q: The 1994 World Cup opening ceremony ended with Diana Ross taking a penalty at a rigged goal. What happened?
a: She missed by a metre and the goal collapsed anyway
note: On film from Soldier Field, 17 June 1994. Retiered ball to extreme, one of the best known bloopers in the game.

q: English referee Andy Wain abandoned a Sunday league match in 2005 after squaring up to a goalkeeper. What had he done first?
a: Sent himself off, saying he would have sent off any player who did that
note: Peterborough Sunday league, January 2005; carried by wire services at the time with Wain's own quote.

q: Colombian midfielder Gerardo Bedoya holds a Guinness record for the wrong reasons. What is it?
a: Most red cards in a professional career, 46
note: Fetched the Guinness page: 46 across a career from 1995 to 2015, and he has retired, so the number will not move.

q: Deportivo needed a last minute penalty on the final day of 1994 to win their first Spanish title. Who missed it?
note: Duplicate of the hardcore extreme question on the same penalty. Kept the hardcore one, which also names him as a defender.

q: A Seville derby in the 2007 Copa del Rey was abandoned and finished behind closed doors in Getafe. Why?
a: Sevilla coach Juande Ramos was knocked unconscious by a bottle thrown from the stand
note: 28 February 2007 at the Benito Villamarin, abandoned after 57 minutes, final 34 minutes played behind closed doors at Getafe's Coliseum Alfonso Perez in March.

q: Atlético Madrid were nearly bankrupt after the Spanish Civil War and merged with another club to survive. Who with?
a: Aviación Nacional, the air force club, making them Atlético Aviación
note: The club's own history page carries the 1939 merger and the Atletico Aviacion name.

q: Spanish goalkeeper Ricardo Zamora was reported shot dead in 1936, then found alive in a Madrid prison. What is said to have kept him there?
a: Playing football with the guards, until the Argentine embassy got him out
note: The false death reports of August 1936 and the Modelo imprisonment are solid. The guards story is traditional rather than documented, which the question already hedges with is said to have, so it is fair as written.

q: When Athletic Bilbao win a major trophy they parade it in a way no other club does. How?
a: On a barge, the gabarra, down the river Nervión into Bilbao
note: Club's own page, and the gabarra sailed again after the 2024 Copa del Rey, which is recent enough to confirm the tradition is live.

q: Barcelona's motto més que un club was not invented by a marketing department. Who said it first, in 1968?
a: Club president Narcís de Carreras, in his nomination speech
note: January 1968 speech on taking the presidency; the attribution is uncontested and appears on Barcelona's own history pages too.

q: After Cruyff's Barcelona won 5-0 at the Bernabéu in February 1974, what did Catalans keep saying to him instead of congratulations?
note: Cruyff told this himself repeatedly and the club's 50th anniversary piece carries it. The match detail (17 February 1974, 5-0) is beyond dispute.

q: Roger Milla was retired and playing on Réunion when he was talked back into the Cameroon squad for the 1990 World Cup. Who talked him round?
a: Paul Biya, the president of Cameroon, who phoned him
note: Britannica and Milla's own interviews both credit the personal call from President Biya.

q: Nottingham Forest won back to back European Cups with a striker Brian Clough had bought for 2,000 pounds from Long Eaton United. What was his day job before that?
a: Carpet fitter, he was Garry Birtles
note: Birtles' fee, the club he came from and the carpet fitting job are all in his own retellings and in Forest's histories.

q: Which club won 6-3 at Ajax's De Meer stadium in April 1980?
note: The match is real (20 April 1980, Ajax 3-6 MVV) but the heaviest ever home defeat framing is not safe: Ajax have since lost 0-4 at home to Feyenoord in 2023 and 0-6 away in 2024, so whether 3-6 still tops the list depends on whether you count margin or goals conceded. Reframed around the scoreline and the ground, which is fixed history.

q: In November 1973 Chile kicked off a World Cup play-off in an empty Estadio Nacional, walked the ball into the net and the referee ended it. Where was the other team?
a: The Soviet Union refused to play in a stadium Pinochet had used as a prison
note: 21 November 1973 walkover, the Soviets having refused after the stadium was used as a detention centre; on the play-off's own article.

q: After Norway beat England in 1981, commentator Bjørge Lillelien listed Lord Nelson, Churchill and Lady Diana before shouting one line at the British prime minister. What?
a: Maggie Thatcher, your boys took a hell of a beating
note: Retiered ball to extreme, the rant is quotable enough that a serious fan produces the line. The quote was one hell of a beating; the recorded line is a hell of a beating. Fixed the wording. The names listed in the question are all in the actual rant.

q: Iceland's thunderclap looks ancient but is not. Where did their fans pick it up?
a: From Motherwell fans, when Stjarnan played at Fir Park in 2014
note: Stjarnan's Europa League tie at Fir Park in 2014, confirmed by both Stjarnan and Motherwell at the time of Euro 2016.

q: Ajax's founders named the club after a Greek warrior for one specific reason. What was it?
a: Ajax killed himself rather than be beaten, so he died unconquered
note: I expected this to be folklore and fetched the source: the ESPN piece on Dutch clubs named from Greek myth gives exactly this reasoning, that Ajax took his own life with Hector's sword and so died unconquered.

q: Sparta Rotterdam's red and white stripes came from a board trip to England in 1899. Which club's kit did they copy?
note: On the club's Wikipedia article and repeated in Sparta's own history; the trip and the Sunderland stripes are the accepted account.

q: Faas Wilkes was banned from the Dutch national team from 1949 to 1955 in his prime. What had he done wrong?
a: Turned professional abroad, which the amateur-only KNVB would not allow
note: The KNVB barred professionals from the national side until Dutch professionalism arrived in the mid 1950s; Wilkes' cap record shows exactly that gap after his 1949 move to Inter.

q: On the last day of the 1999 season, Carlisle United needed a goal in the final seconds to stay in the Football League. Who scored it?
a: Their on-loan goalkeeper Jimmy Glass, who had come up for a corner
note: 8 May 1999 against Plymouth, in the second minute of stoppage time; one of the best documented moments in English lower league football.

q: Real Madrid went into the final day one point clear in both 1992 and 1993, and lost the title both times to the same opponent. Who kept beating them?
note: Duplicate of the hardcore extreme question on the same two final days, with the same answer. Kept the hardcore one.
